solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicators.note: the peg sits inside the word for fixed, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: set means fixed or settled, as in set in stone
a pin is a small peg

explanation.surface: A tuning peg lodged inside an old keyboard instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'Fixed' as describing the peg, but it is its own piece that goes around it. Fittingly, harpsichords really do have tuning pins.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinet is a small kind of harpsichord, so the definition is a broader category naming this instrument.

clue.text: Small apple I left out for armed soldier

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

indicators.note: left out means omitted, so the letter I is dropped from the apple's name

parts.note: the pearmain is an old variety of apple
the letter to be removed from the apple

explanation.surface: A soldier is sent off with a small apple for his rations, oddly minus one of its parts.
explanation.walkthrough: The apple here is a named variety, not a generic synonym; Worcester Pearmain is a common English eating apple.
explanation.definitionFit: A spearman is a soldier carrying a spear, so an armed fighting man in the older military sense.

indicators.note: something battered has been knocked out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, matching the enumeration

explanation.surface: Worn old dice with Latin markings all look the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battered' looks like a description of the dice, but it is the instruction to rearrange 'Latin dice'.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that are identical are exactly the same as each other, which is a plain synonym relation.

clue.text: New statue now and again reveals OT character

indicators.note: now and again means at regular intervals, so only every other letter is taken

parts.note: the even letters of these two words, starting from the second

explanation.surface: A freshly unveiled statue that occasionally shows a Bible figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Take letters 2, 4, 6 and 8 of NEWSTATUE. OT is the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: Esau is the elder twin brother of Jacob in Genesis, a figure from the Old Testament books.

clue.text: Dull bank payment system backed cover

indicators.note: backed means moved backwards, so the joined pieces are read from right to left

parts.note: drab means dull and colourless
BACS is the British automated clearing system banks use for direct debits and salaries

explanation.surface: A boring banking system that has been given support and insurance cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' pretends to mean supported financially, which suits the bank; in fact it is the instruction to read the pieces backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A scabbard is the sheath that encloses a sword blade, so it is a protective cover for a weapon.

parts.note: surface reading: the idiom for something that is exactly what one likes
setter's reading: taken literally, a brew is a hot drink made by steeping leaves

explanation.walkthrough: The British idiom 'just my cup of tea' means exactly to my taste; the clue plays it against the literal drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A brew is British slang for a pot of the hot leaf drink, so the literal phrase names one serving.

parts.note: a bald statement is plain and blunt, so balder means more obvious
to career is to rush along headlong, as does to dash

explanation.surface: A job for shoemakers that is plainer than another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Career' reads as a noun (a job) but is the verb to speed. Cobblers is British slang for nonsense, not just shoemakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobblers in British slang means rubbish talk, and balderdash is senseless talk too, so both are synonyms.

parts.note: used as it stands
the head is the top of something, as at the head of a page

explanation.walkthrough: 'Top up' looks like refilling a glass; split it so 'A top' is the wordplay and 'up' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A team that is two goals up is leading in the score, the same sense as being in front.

indicators.note: the opponents are placed in the word for dreadful, which surrounds them

parts.note: dire means dreadful or terrible
in bridge East and South sit on opposing sides of the table

explanation.surface: Someone badly lacking any opponents to play a game with.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, North–South play East–West, so any compass pair from different partnerships, like E and S, are opponents.
explanation.definitionFit: Desire as a noun is a strong wish or craving, a synonym for want in the sense of longing.

definitions.note: plural noun for a collective singular one

indicators.note: being told something is hearing it, so the word for sheets is taken by its sound

parts.note: a quire is a set of 24 or 25 sheets of paper

explanation.surface: Singers who carry their sheet music, or so we hear.
explanation.walkthrough: QUIRE, a paper-trade measure, is pronounced exactly like the singing group.
explanation.definitionFit: A choir is an organised group of singers, so it is a collective body of vocalists performing together.

clue.text: Viewer lived next to Henry. Rot!

parts.note: the eye is the organ that views
to have lived is to have been, as in 'there was a king'
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A television viewer who lived next door to Henry, dismissed as nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Viewer' suggests a TV audience member, but it is simply the eye. 'Next to' only strings the pieces together.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyewash is informal for nonsense meant to deceive, and rot is exclaimed to dismiss claims as rubbish.

indicators.note: a ruined building has fallen apart, so its letters lie in a new order

parts.note: seven letters of fodder

explanation.surface: Decorative drapery salvaged from crumbling ancient shrines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Valances' could be either curtain word; the fodder settles which. Pelmets are the boxed strips above a curtain.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelmets are the short fabric or wooden strips hiding curtain rails, which the British also call valances.

indicators.note: a resident lives inside, so the name is the inner part of the country's full name

parts.note: GB stands for Great Britain; spell the country out and keep its inside letters

explanation.surface: A young woman who lives in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters are not in the clue itself: expand GB to the country's name first, then drop its first letter and last two.
explanation.definitionFit: Crosswords routinely clue any female first name with girl, and this is a common woman's name.

indicators.note: a collapse brings a structure tumbling down, so its letters fall into a new order

parts.note: ten letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A camera catches a player's dreadful dive on the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a player diving for a penalty; 'collapse of' is really the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A midfielder is a soccer player positioned between defence and attack, one kind of football player.

clue.text: Cutlery item from a fete Kinks organised

indicators.note: to organise is to arrange, so the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: ten letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A piece of cutlery from a village fair put on by the 1960s rock band the Kinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kinks are a British band, but here only their letters matter. A fete is a village fundraising fair.
explanation.definitionFit: A steak knife is a sharp serrated table knife for cutting meat, so it belongs among cutlery.

indicators.note: the name is lodged in the run of letters across the next words

parts.note: the tail of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: An American writer living in a country cottage.
explanation.walkthrough: Found in rur(AL COTT)age, spanning the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: Louisa May Alcott was the American author of Little Women, so she is a novelist from the United States.

clue.text: Roosevelt's plan for naked swimmer is reported

indicators.note: a report is heard, so the naked swimmer is taken by sound

parts.note: naked is nude, and an eel is a swimmer

explanation.surface: A president's scheme concerning skinny-dippers.
explanation.walkthrough: Every eel is naked, which is the joke: NUDE EEL said aloud runs together into the historic programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal was his 1930s programme of economic recovery reforms in Depression-era America.

parts.note: aqua is a greenish-blue colour
a plane is a carpenter's tool for smoothing wood

explanation.surface: A turquoise-coloured tool for making a playground chute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slide' reads as a noun, but it is the verb: a car's tyres skid across water on the road.
explanation.definitionFit: To aquaplane is for a vehicle to skid uncontrollably on a film of surface water, so to slide.

indicators.note: redistributing hands things out again in a new arrangement, so the letters are reordered
non means without, so the letter U is removed from the treasure word

parts.note: nine letters before one is removed

explanation.surface: A regime reclaims control by sharing out the vulgar classes' riches.
explanation.walkthrough: Non-U is British slang for not upper-class, which is why it sits with redistribution; here it just strips a U.
explanation.definitionFit: To reassert something is to state or enforce it again, so to impose authority once more after a lapse.

clue.text: Carpet from university residence is spoken of

indicators.note: what is spoken is heard rather than read, so the residence is taken by sound

parts.note: Keele Hall is the mansion at Keele University in Staffordshire; a hall is also student housing

explanation.surface: A rug taken from a student hall that people talk about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpet' is the British verb to reprimand, not a floor covering. Keele is an English university town.
explanation.definitionFit: To keelhaul was a naval punishment dragging a sailor under the hull; figuratively it means rebuke severely.

clue.text: Wrapped up warmly, with the truth well hidden

definitions.meaning: concealed or disguised, as in secrecy

explanation.surface: Bundled up against the cold while keeping the facts secret.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves describe the same word: one literal (in a heavy cape), one figurative (veiled in secrecy).
explanation.definitionFit: To be cloaked is literally to wear a cape, and figuratively to be veiled in secrecy or disguise.

clue.text: Quell any doubts of Jenny going by river

parts.note: a jenny is a female donkey
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire, a crossword regular

explanation.surface: Calming someone's worries about a woman called Jenny travelling by the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jenny' looks like a woman's name but is the female donkey; 'going by' just places one piece beside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To assure someone is to remove their uncertainty by giving confident promises, so to settle their worries.

clue.text: Arrives hurriedly and gets into debt?

definitions.meaning: someone who dashes over to you comes rushing along
as in running up a bill or overdraft

explanation.surface: Someone who dashes in and then overspends.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second meaning is a stretch of the same phrasal verb, as in running up a bar tab.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb covers both approaching at speed and accumulating charges like a bar tab.

indicators.note: the power symbol is put in the word for pile-drivers, which wraps round it

parts.note: a ram is a heavy weight used to drive piles into the ground
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: Boosting the power of the machines that hammer building piles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upgrades' is a noun here: slopes going upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A ramp is a sloping surface joining two levels, so an upgrade in the sense of an uphill incline.

clue.text: Zaniest UK bishop out in Tashkent's land

indicators.note: out means disordered or off kilter, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: fodder, taken as printed
fodder, taken as printed
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: A wildly eccentric British bishop out and about in Central Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' looks like part of the story (the bishop is out travelling) but is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Tashkent is the capital city of Uzbekistan, so the country is the nation where that city lies.

clue.text: The Sheep-Pig has left making a confused noise

parts.note: Babe is the pig hero of Dick King-Smith's novel The Sheep-Pig, later the film Babe
L is the usual abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: The piglet star of a children's story has gone, leaving a racket behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has left' reads as departed, but it means the pig has an L attached.
explanation.definitionFit: A babel is a din of many voices, after the biblical tower where languages were confounded.

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the next word is taken

parts.note: the letters after the first one

explanation.surface: A rather useless motor manufacturer.
explanation.walkthrough: Found in h(OPEL)ess.
explanation.definitionFit: Opel is the German automobile manufacturer, long owned by General Motors, so it is a motor company.

clue.text: Not my report from the old days

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the word for the old days is taken by sound

parts.note: yore means long ago, as in days of yore

explanation.surface: Disowning a school report card from years gone by.
explanation.walkthrough: In many British accents YORE and YOUR are said the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: The possessive belonging to the listener rather than the speaker is the opposite of the first-person form.

indicators.note: in play the letters are moving about, so they come out in a new order

parts.note: seven letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A musician boasting about their wonderful blues performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blues' looks like the music, or a sports team; it is only letters, with 'I'm' joining the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Sublime describes something of such excellence or beauty it inspires awe, like a magnificent sight.

clue.text: Commensurate backing in Qatar or Pakistan

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the hidden letters are read right to left
the phrase is lodged in the run of letters across the country names

parts.note: the tail of the first country, the whole of 'or', and the first letter of the second

explanation.surface: Proportionate financial support available in two Asian countries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' pretends to be financial support; it reverses q(ATAR OR P)akistan.
explanation.definitionFit: Pro rata is Latin for in proportion, so an amount calculated that way is commensurate with its share.

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters come out altered in order

parts.note: eight letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A metal cooking pot bubbling away, then a curious mention of an official tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' also hints that the answer is fudged. The cabbage palmetto is the official tree of Florida and South Carolina.
explanation.definitionFit: The palmetto is a fan palm designated as the emblem tree of two American states, hence a state tree.

clue.text: Gold? It's lead in disguise, severe test shows

parts.note: or is the heraldic term for gold

indicators.note: a disguise changes how something looks, so the metal's letters appear in another order

parts.note: fodder, taken as printed

explanation.surface: An alchemist's fake: the gold is only lead dressed up, as rigorous testing reveals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' just glues gold to the disguised metal. The surface is alchemy in reverse, but OR plus a jumble of LEAD does it.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordeal is a painful or harrowing experience, and historically a trial by fire or water, so a hard trial.
